name: Mikhail Khodorkovsky

summary.text: Mikhail Khodorkovsky is a former Russian businessman who headed the bank Menatep and later the oil company Yukos, which a company controlled by him and his partners acquired in the 1995 loans-for-shares auction. He was arrested on October 25, 2003 while Yukos's chief executive, convicted in 2005 and again in December 2010, and pardoned by President Vladimir Putin on December 20, 2013 after about ten years in custody. In January 2020 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that his second trial had violated his fair-trial rights, while declining to find that the prosecution was politically motivated.

facts.claim: In the 1995 loans-for-shares auction of Yukos, Khodorkovsky's bank Menatep was put in charge of processing the bids; the winner was a company controlled by Khodorkovsky and his partners, and a rival bid from three large Russian banks that offered more money was disqualified on technical grounds. Bloomberg reported in April 1996 that Menatep was putting up $350 million, which it called about half the company's estimated worth; The Moscow Times at the time described Yukos as Russia's second-largest oil company.
facts.quote: Khodorkovsky's Menatep was put in charge of processing the bids in the Yukos auction, and the winner turned out to be a company controlled by … Khodorkovsky and his partners. A rival bid by three big Russian banks, which offered more money than Khodorkovsky's outfit, was disqualified on technical grounds.

facts.claim: Bloomberg reported in April 1996 that Khodorkovsky was stepping down as Menatep's chief executive while remaining its chairman and would probably become a first vice-president of Yukos. RFE/RL later described him as the person who built Yukos into what became Russia's largest oil company and as its chief executive at the time of his arrest.
facts.quote: he's stepping down as Menatep's CEO while remaining its chairman. He will probably become a first vice-president of Yukos.

facts.claim: Khodorkovsky, then Yukos's chief executive, was arrested on a Siberian airstrip on October 25, 2003.

facts.claim: Khodorkovsky was convicted in 2005, about two years after his arrest, on charges reported as fraud and tax evasion; reports give the resulting prison term as eight years (CNBC) or nine years (The Moscow Times).
facts.quote: after two years on remand, Khodorkovsky was jailed for eight years in 2005

facts.claim: In December 2010 Khodorkovsky was convicted in a second trial of embezzlement and laundering the proceeds; his combined prison term rose to 13 years and was reduced to 11 years by the Moscow City Court in December 2012, with release scheduled for August 2014.
facts.quote: before being reduced to 11 years by the Moscow City Court last December

facts.claim: President Vladimir Putin said on December 19, 2013 that he would pardon Khodorkovsky, citing humanitarian circumstances and his mother's illness. Putin signed the pardon on Friday, December 20, 2013; it took effect immediately, and Khodorkovsky was released from a prison in Segezha and flew to Germany.
facts.quote: On Friday, Putin signed the order pardoning Khodorkovsky and it immediately went into effect

facts.claim: Putin's spokesman said Khodorkovsky's request for clemency implied an admission of guilt; Khodorkovsky said the issue of admission of guilt was not raised, and said days after his release that he had no plans to return to Russia.

facts.claim: In January 2020 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the trial judge's refusal to let the defence examine witnesses and evidence in Khodorkovsky's second trial violated his right to a fair trial; the court did not find that the prosecution was politically motivated and ordered no compensation.

openQuestions: Sentence lengths differ between reports: the 2005 term is given as eight years (CNBC) or nine years (The Moscow Times); the original nine-year sentence is widely said to have been cut to eight on appeal, but that step was not in the pages returned. The 2005 charges are described variously as fraud and tax evasion or as embezzlement and money laundering; the court names and the exact counts were not captured.

The 1995 price: Bloomberg (April 1996) says Menatep put up $350 million; one returned passage gives $350 million for 78% of Yukos without its source being identified; The Moscow Times headline says the 'managed' sale fetched $160 million (possibly the loan stage rather than the later investment tender). The Moscow Times archive page's date was not shown.
The site lists Khodorkovsky among 'insiders' of a Harvard HIID/USAID-designed loans-for-shares scheme; none of the pages returned connects him, Menatep or the Yukos auction to Harvard HIID or USAID.

The quoted PBS Frontline/World passage was returned by the search tool alongside a Washington Post 2003 opinion column; confirm it is from the PBS page. 'Rigged' characterisations of the auction appear in the returned text as critics' views and are not recorded as fact.

Khodorkovsky's own shareholding in Yukos/Group Menatep and the later ownership of the arbitration claimants (Hulley Enterprises, Yukos Universal, Veteran Petroleum) were not researched; see yukos.json. His current residence (reported as London) was returned only in a search summary of the January 2020 coverage.
The pardon decree itself (kremlin.ru) was not opened; the pardon is recorded from NBC, RFE/RL, The Moscow Times and CNBC.
